paper_title: A computational search for the optimal microelectronic heat sink using ANSYS Icepak

scenario.figure_or_table: Table 1 and Fig. 1 (geometry); Table 3 (boundary conditions, PDF p.4); Table 6 (source temperature, PDF p.11)
scenario.description: Inline-arrangement (IA) circular pin-fin aluminium heat sink with 36 fins cooling a single 2.2 x 2.2 x 0.1 cm chip in a 6 x 5 x 2 cm cabinet, solved in ANSYS Icepak (FLUENT solver). The chip dissipates 8 W. Air enters at 0.1 m/s and 298 K, and all other cabinet surfaces are insulated. The paper reports a maximum source temperature of 126.97 C for this case (Table 6, PDF p.11), measured as the source maximum temperature and used to compute thermal resistance Rth = (Ts - Tin)/Q. The paper publishes only chip, heat sink and cabinet dimensions and a single 8 W power. It gives no block placement coordinates and no power time series, and it has no linked repository or supplementary data (the data availability statement says no data was used). The paper's own dimensions are inconsistent: Table 1 gives a 4 x 4 x 1.7 cm heat sink, while the text gives a 3 x 3.5 x 2 cm base with 1.5 cm fins of 0.16 cm radius, against a Table 1 fin diameter of 0.2 cm.
scenario.architecture: Air-cooled single-chip package: a 2.2 x 2.2 x 0.1 cm heat source on a substrate board, with an aluminium pin-fin heat sink (36 circular fins, inline) inside a 6 x 5 x 2 cm enclosure. It is not a chiplet, 2.5D or 3D-stacked system.
scenario.workload: Constant 8 W uniform heat load on the single chip, applied as a steady heat source at the bottom wall of the heat sink.
scenario.operating_point: Steady state; inlet velocity 0.1 m/s; inlet air temperature 298 K; 8 W; outlet at pressure boundary; other cabinet walls adiabatic. Reported maximum source temperature 126.97 C (IA circular, Table 6). Reported pressure drop 0.12 (Table 7; units not stated in the extracted text).

original_setup.solver: ANSYS Icepak (FLUENT solver), 3D steady-state, pressure-based, implicit CFD with realizable k-epsilon turbulence model and standard wall functions; velocity inlet and pressure outlet (PDF p.3 Table 2, PDF p.5, PDF p.6)
original_setup.optimizer: None. The paper is a parametric comparison of fin cross-section (circular vs conical) and arrangement (inline vs staggered), with no automated optimizer, so 'optimal' means choosing the best of four fixed cases (PDF p.1, PDF p.11)
original_setup.controller: None. Constant 8 W heat load, 0.1 m/s inlet velocity and 298 K inlet air temperature, with no dynamic or feedback controller (PDF p.4 Table 3)
original_setup.benchmark: Selected scenario: inline (IA) circular pin-fin aluminium heat sink, 36 fins, cooling a single 2.2 x 2.2 x 0.1 cm chip in a 6 x 5 x 2 cm cabinet. The solver is validated against Adhikari et al. experiments (deviation under 3.68%, Fig. 6, PDF p.6 and p.8) and against Rosli et al. numerical results (Table 5, PDF p.6: IA 107.43 C vs 106.474 C, SA 101.85 C vs 101.662 C). The paper has no linked repository, supplementary data or pinned assets; the data availability statement says no data was used (PDF p.11).

thermal_observable.location: Maximum temperature of the heat source (chip) for the inline circular pin-fin case; the thermal resistance formula uses the maximum temperature on the fin base relative to inlet air (Eq. 7-8, PDF p.6)
thermal_observable.aggregation: Spatial maximum over the source from the steady-state CFD solution. Reported in Table 6 (Inline IA, circular) and used for Rth = (Ts - Tin)/Q.

physical_mismatches.reason: The setup is a 3D conjugate CFD model with forced air convection through an enclosed cabinet (0.1 m/s inlet, pressure outlet, insulated walls). It has no chiplets, interposer or 3D stack, and a steady 2D conduction-only Studio model cannot represent the 3D airflow, fin geometry, pressure drop or velocity fields.

The cooling is a 36-pin aluminium finned heat sink with air flow. A bundled Studio package/material stack does not include these pin fins or the airflow, so the cooling path and boundary conditions differ essentially.

The paper's dimensions are internally inconsistent: Table 1 gives a 4 x 4 x 1.7 cm heat sink and a 0.2 cm fin diameter, while the text gives a 3 x 3.5 x 2 cm base, 1.5 cm fin height and 0.16 cm fin radius. The geometry is ambiguous.

The paper contains no block placement coordinates. Only the chip footprint, the heat sink and cabinet sizes, and a single 8 W power are published, so any 2D placement would be an illustrative construction and not paper-derived.
The paper runs a steady-state analysis with a constant 8 W load. It provides no transient power trace, no controller and no optimizer, so any one-row power trace is not a published workload.

The paper reports a maximum chip temperature of 126.97 C with 298 K inlet air and a 0.1 m/s flow rate. It assumes constant material properties and neglects radiation and gravity. Studio temperatures cannot be compared numerically with this value.

Table 3 and the boundary-condition text are ambiguous about where the heat is applied, whether to the heat sink bottom wall or the chip, and about an unspecified substrate board. Reported mesh sizes and solver details (Table 4) do not map to a Studio solver.

studio_assumptions: Bundled Studio package/material assumptions are not specified in the supplied packet and are not paper-derived; they would be a separate 2D conduction model with its own package and material properties.
A runner may construct a separate illustrative 2D placement of the 2.2 x 2.2 cm chip footprint with 8 W and a one-row power trace; such coordinates are generated and not paper facts.
Studio temperatures must not be compared numerically with the paper's 126.97 C value.
No exact replication is claimed. No floorplan blocks are asserted as paper-derived, because no placement coordinates exist.
